units.title: Modern Chinese Art: Finding New Paths
units.intro: In the early 20th century, facing the impact of Western art, Chinese painters tried different ways to 'modernise' Chinese painting.

lessons.title: The Lingnan School's Innovations
cards: The Lingnan School (嶺南畫派) arose in Guangdong in the early 20th century. Its founders, Gao Jianfu (高劍父), Gao Qifeng (高奇峰) and Chen Shuren (陳樹人), are known as the 'Two Gaos and One Chen'.
Gao Jianfu (高劍父) and Chen Shuren (陳樹人) first studied painting under Ju Lian (居廉); Gao Qifeng (高奇峰) learned from his elder brother Gao Jianfu. All three later studied in Japan.
They called for 'blending Chinese and Western, uniting old and new', painting new subjects such as aeroplanes, tanks and other modern things.
In technique, they valued 'water-splashing and powder-splashing' (撞水撞粉), which makes flower-and-bird colours look moist and luminous.
The Lingnan School (嶺南畫派) deeply influenced Hong Kong. Painters such as Chao Shao-an (趙少昂) brought it to Hong Kong and developed it further.

quiz.question: Who is NOT one of the Lingnan School's 'Two Gaos and One Chen'?
quiz.explain: Xu Beihong followed the path of realism and was not a founder of the Lingnan School.

quiz.question: What did the Lingnan School advocate?
options: Blending Chinese and Western, uniting old and new
quiz.answer: Blending Chinese and Western, uniting old and new
quiz.explain: They wanted to keep the brush and ink of Chinese painting while taking in foreign techniques and new subjects.

quiz.question: The Lingnan technique that makes colours moist and luminous is called 'water-splashing and ____'.
quiz.explain: 'Water-splashing and powder-splashing' was developed by Ju Lian and taken up by the Lingnan School.

quiz.question: In which country did Lingnan School painters study and pick up new techniques?
quiz.explain: Gao Jianfu and others studied in Japan, absorbing Japanese painting and Western realist techniques.

lessons.title: Xu Beihong and Realism
cards: Xu Beihong (徐悲鴻, 1895–1953) studied in France at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, learning Western academic drawing and oil painting.
He believed Chinese painting needed 'reform', and argued that Western realist drawing should be the foundation for depicting form.
His most famous subject is galloping horses, painted in ink with accurate anatomy to show strength and speed.
Major works include the oil painting Tian Heng and His Five Hundred Followers (《田橫五百士》), which uses a historical story to express national integrity.
After 1949 he became the first president of the Central Academy of Fine Arts (中央美術學院). His realist teaching system shaped Chinese art education for many years.

quiz.question: What is Xu Beihong's most famous ink-painting subject?
quiz.explain: He used realist knowledge of anatomy to paint horses, with bold brushwork and accurate structure.

quiz.question: What did Xu Beihong say should be the foundation of form in Chinese painting?
quiz.explain: He believed drawing was the foundation of all visual art.

quiz.question: Match each work to its type
options: Tian Heng and His Five Hundred Followers
quiz.explain: Xu Beihong worked in both oil and ink.

quiz.question: After 1949, Xu Beihong became the first president of which school?
quiz.explain: His realist teaching system spread from there.

lessons.title: Lin Fengmian's Fusion
cards: Lin Fengmian (林風眠, 1900–1991) studied in France and was strongly influenced by Western modernism, such as Fauvism and Cubism.
In 1928 he founded the National Academy of Art (國立藝術院) in Hangzhou, today's China Academy of Art, promoting 'harmonising Chinese and Western art'.
He often used square compositions, combining ink, watercolour and rich colour. His subjects include ladies, still lifes, egrets and autumn scenes.
His students included Wu Guanzhong (吳冠中), Zao Wou-Ki (趙無極) and Chu Teh-Chun (朱德群), who all became important modern artists.
In his later years he settled in Hong Kong, where he kept creating art until his death.

quiz.question: Where did Lin Fengmian found the National Academy of Art?
quiz.explain: Founded in 1928, it is today's China Academy of Art.

quiz.question: Which of these was NOT a student of Lin Fengmian?
quiz.explain: Gao Jianfu was a founder of the Lingnan School and older than Lin Fengmian.

quiz.question: Which composition format is common in Lin Fengmian's work?
quiz.explain: The square format broke away from traditional Chinese scroll formats and is close to the Western idea of a framed picture.

quiz.question: Lin Fengmian promoted '____ Chinese and Western art'.
quiz.explain: He wanted to combine the spirit of Chinese art with modern Western forms.

lessons.title: Wu Guanzhong and Formal Beauty
cards: Wu Guanzhong (吳冠中, 1919–2010) studied under Lin Fengmian (林風眠) at the National Hangzhou Academy of Art, then went to study in Paris.
He valued 'formal beauty' (形式美): dots, lines, planes and colours are beautiful in themselves, so a painting need not be realistic.
He often painted Jiangnan (江南) water towns: white walls, black tiles, curving lines and dots of colour, in simple, rhythmic pictures.
In 1992 he published 'Brush and Ink Equal Zero' (〈筆墨等於零〉), arguing that brush and ink must serve the picture and are worthless on their own. It caused huge debate.
He painted in both oil and ink, aiming to 'give oil painting a national character and modernise Chinese painting'.

quiz.question: What did Wu Guanzhong paint most often?
quiz.explain: White walls and black tiles provide the formal elements of dot, line and plane.

quiz.question: In 1992 Wu Guanzhong published an essay called 'Brush and Ink Equal ____'.
quiz.explain: He argued that brush and ink are worthless apart from the picture, which sparked a big debate.

quiz.question: What does 'formal beauty' mainly emphasise?
options: The beauty of dots, lines, planes and colour themselves
quiz.answer: The beauty of dots, lines, planes and colour themselves
quiz.explain: Formal beauty focuses on the picture's elements and how they are organised.

quiz.question: Who was Wu Guanzhong's teacher?
quiz.explain: He studied under Lin Fengmian at the National Hangzhou Academy of Art.

lessons.title: Zao Wou-Ki and Abstraction
cards: Zao Wou-Ki (趙無極, 1920–2013) studied under Lin Fengmian (林風眠) at the National Hangzhou Academy of Art, and moved to Paris in 1948.
Early on he was inspired by Paul Klee (保羅·克利), and symbols like oracle bone script (甲骨文) appeared in his paintings.
He later developed lyrical abstraction: large fields of colour and flowing brushstrokes that evoke landscapes, light and the universe.
Many works are titled by completion date, such as June–October 1985 (《1985年6月-10月》), so viewers don't read them as specific subjects.
In 2002 he was elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts (法蘭西藝術院) in France. He is a leading figure of abstract art fusing East and West.

quiz.question: Which city did Zao Wou-Ki move to in 1948?
quiz.explain: In Paris he encountered modern Western art and developed his abstract style.

quiz.question: Which Western artist inspired Zao Wou-Ki early in his career?
quiz.explain: Klee's symbols and lines inspired him to add symbols like oracle bone script.

quiz.question: How did Zao Wou-Ki title many of his works?
quiz.explain: Date titles make viewers focus on colour and space, not a specific subject.

quiz.question: Match each artist to their style
quiz.explain: All three wanted to modernise Chinese art, but in different ways.

quiz.question: How does Zao Wou-Ki's work show a fusion of East and West?
options: Using oil paint to express the mood of Chinese landscape
Only copying ancient paintings in ink
quiz.answer: Using oil paint to express the mood of Chinese landscape
quiz.explain: A Western medium combined with Eastern ideas of space and qiyun (spirit resonance).

units.title: Hong Kong Art and Identity
units.intro: From New Ink to contemporary practice, Hong Kong artists respond to the city, identity and collecting spaces—aligned with Form 6 themes (Self / Tradition / Society) and museum visits (HK Palace Museum, Xubaizhai).

lessons.title: New Ink: Lui Shou-kwan and Wucius Wong
cards: Lui Shou-kwan (1919–1975) was a key force in Hong Kong New Ink, refining landscape into bold ink masses and voids with a Zen, abstract lean.
Rather than only copying models, he used modern composition and simplified form so ink could speak about mind-states, not just scenery.
Wucius Wong, inspired by Lui, joined design-like structure to ink, stressing order, layering and geometry.
New Ink helped post-war Hong Kong build a local modern ink language—an important chapter of artistic identity.
(Pending teacher review) Use a visual diary to note how void and ink mass can carry emotion.

quiz.question: Hong Kong’s modern ink movement linked to Lui is usually called?
quiz.explain: Lui is a major New Ink pioneer in Hong Kong.

quiz.question: A formal trait often seen in Lui’s work is?
quiz.explain: Abstracted landscape with breathing empty space.

quiz.question: Wucius Wong’s ink often stresses design-like ＿＿ and layers.
quiz.explain: He brings design thinking into ink.

quiz.question: Why does New Ink matter for HK identity?
options: It built a local modern ink language
quiz.answer: It built a local modern ink language

lessons.title: Luis Chan’s Surreal Hong Kong
cards: Luis Chan (1905–1995) began with more naturalistic views and portraits; from the 1960s his art turned fantastical and surreal.
Bright colour, naïve forms and dream logic turn Hong Kong hills and harbour into imagined worlds.
Humour and folk-like play challenge the idea that Hong Kong art must only document reality.
For DSE students he models surreal strategies for “everyday city + inner feeling”.
(Pending teacher review) Maps to this unit’s “explore surreal life” aim.

quiz.question: About when did Luis Chan shift toward surreal fantasy?
A common trait of his surreal work is?
He often treats Hong Kong’s ＿＿ through surreal invention.
quiz.explain: City and hills become dream scenes.

quiz.question: Match

lessons.title: Contemporary HK identity: Pak, Lee Kit, Wilson Shieh
cards: Pak Sheung Chuen uses conceptual gestures and everyday materials to make pressure of housing and city space thinkable.
Lee Kit builds quiet installations with painting, cloth, projection and domestic objects—private, fragile moments.
Wilson Shieh paints contemporary figures in gongbi colour; faces may be blank or role-like, probing identity and gender.
Concept, spatial sensing and figuration—all ask who we are and how we live here.
(Pending teacher review) Ties to this unit’s “Self…society” theme and role-taking.

quiz.question: Pak’s approach is closest to?

lessons.title: Museums and local collections: HKPM & Xubaizhai
cards: The Hong Kong Palace Museum stages exhibitions tied to Palace Museum culture—useful for material culture and aesthetics.
The Xubaizhai Collection at the Hong Kong Museum of Art centres Chinese painting and calligraphy for literati study.
A visit is observation practice: composition, colophons, seals, mounting and display narratives.
This unit links these visits to self-review and portfolio; keep a visual diary of questions.
(Pending teacher review) Prompt: how do traditional symbols enter life in Hong Kong today?

quiz.question: Xubaizhai is best known for?
HK Palace Museum mainly helps students?
options: Meet Chinese artefacts and exhibition narratives
quiz.answer: Meet Chinese artefacts and exhibition narratives

quiz.question: In museums, practise ＿＿ and questions—not only photos.

quiz.explain: Stated in this unit’s learning aims.

units.title: Introduction to Western Modernism
units.intro: From Impressionism to abstraction, then a bridge to postmodern identity, Cindy Sherman and the YBA—matching this unit’s learning aims.

lessons.title: Impressionism and Post-Impressionism: Monet and Van Gogh
cards: Impressionists prized outdoor light, visible brushwork and fleeting colour over polished academic finish.
Claude Monet’s Impression, Sunrise (1872) and Water Lilies explore changing light and reflection.
Vincent van Gogh pushed high chroma and swirling stroke so touch itself carries feeling.
Both unsettled “likeness alone” as the only standard and opened doors to modernism.
(Pending teacher review) A light link to ink “stroke as feeling” can wait for U5.

quiz.question: Who painted Impression, Sunrise?
A van Gogh hallmark is?
Impressionism hunts ＿＿ changes of light and colour.
A key impact was?

lessons.title: Fauvism and Cubism: Matisse and Picasso
cards: Henri Matisse and the Fauves used intense, non-natural colour and simplified shape.
Pablo Picasso and Braque built Cubism by fracturing forms into multi-view planes.
Les Demoiselles d’Avignon (1907) is an early Cubist landmark breaking stable perspective.
Modernism could reinvent seeing through colour or through structural analysis.
(Pending teacher review) Pair with Tate “human figure” resources.

quiz.question: Fauvism emphasises?
Cubism often?
Les Demoiselles d’Avignon dates to about ＿＿.
Match

lessons.title: Paths to abstraction: Kandinsky, Mondrian, Rothko
cards: Wassily Kandinsky argued colour and shape can free themselves from objects; Concerning the Spiritual in Art was influential.
Piet Mondrian’s Neo-Plasticism uses horizontals, verticals and primary colours for balance.
Mark Rothko’s colour-field paintings immerse viewers in soft-edged fields of feeling.
Abstraction is organised meaning—not “anything goes”.
(Pending teacher review) Cross-link Wu Guanzhong / Zao Wou-Ki later.

quiz.question: Kandinsky linked abstraction to?
Mondrian’s language is often?
Rothko often uses large ＿＿ colour fields.
Abstraction’s key is?

lessons.title: Postmodern identity: Sherman and the YBA
cards: Postmodern work often questions “authentic identity” and originality via appropriation and role-play.
Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Stills (1977–1980) stages typed female roles to probe gaze and representation.

Pop Art paved the way for postmodernism: Andy Warhol used silkscreen printing to repeat images of celebrities and consumer goods, as in Marilyn Diptych (1962), questioning originality and the value of the handmade.
The YBA emerged in 1990s Britain; Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin became widely known for startling materials and autobiographical strategies.
This bridge lesson supports this unit’s role-taking aim: “Reappear someone in Chinese context”.
(Pending teacher review) Extend with Tate “changed identity” / “human figure”.

quiz.question: Sherman’s key strategy is?
YBA refers to?

units.title: Contemporary Chinese Art
units.intro: Bridge from Xu Beihong and Qi Baishi into Xu Bing, Political Pop, installation/performance and video—aligned with F.5 Art Talk and global contemporary views.

lessons.title: Bridge: Xu Beihong and Qi Baishi toward today
cards: Xu Beihong championed academic drawing; horses and history subjects tied structure to national meaning.
Qi Baishi brought folk-flavoured birds, fish and insects into modern viewership.
Later artists inherit these “modern classics” while facing globalisation and new media.
Seeing realist pedagogy and folk wit first makes later refusals and appropriations clearer.
(Pending teacher review) Detail on Xu also sits in U1.

quiz.answer: A bridge from modern to contemporary

lessons.title: Xu Bing: writing, concept, calligraphy currents
cards: Book from the Sky (1980s) prints invented pseudo-characters, unsettling trust in writing.
Language, reading and cultural misreading link conceptual art to calligraphic tradition.
F.5 Art Talk pairs Xu Bing with contemporary Chinese calligraphy currents and global art.
Students may translate the idea of a broken writing system into school, net or dialect barriers.
(Pending teacher review) Transform the concept—do not only copy pseudo-glyphs for marks.

lessons.title: Political Pop and Cynical Realism
cards: Wang Guangyi’s Great Criticism-type works juxtapose propaganda imagery with consumer logos.
Yue Minjun’s laughing figures and Fang Lijun’s bald heads are discussed in Cynical Realism contexts.
They respond to memory, consumption and mood after Reform—not “pretty painting” alone.
Compare carefully with Warhol’s mass-image tactics (U5); contexts differ.

lessons.title: Installation, performance and video
cards: Cai Guo-Qiang is known for gunpowder drawings and explosion events—ephemeral mark and spectacle.
Zhang Huan and others use the body as medium under social gaze.
Zhang Peili is a key early video figure; Yang Fudong works with cinematic time; Cao Fei explores virtual worlds and subcultures.
New media lets the work be process, event or virtual space.
(Pending teacher review) Aligns with F.5 global contemporary talk.

units.title: East–West Comparative Perspectives
units.intro: Practise cross-cultural comparison: symbols, role-taking, and how YBA/American contemporary relate to Chinese art—per F.6. Full Ming–Qing survey is U6 backlog.

lessons.title: Method: same, difference, borrow
cards: Good comparison is not “who wins”; describe and analyse form before context and meaning.

lessons.title: Symbols: literati cues meet today (U6 preview)
cards: Ming–Qing literati painting uses birds, strange rocks, colophons and brush habits as moral/feeling signs; Bada Shanren’s creatures are often read with loyalist anguish.
Wu School figures such as Shen Zhou and Wen Zhengming stress poetry–calligraphy–painting unity; Xu Wei and Chen Chun push freer xieyi ink.
Contemporaries may reuse or deliberately misalign these signs for present issues.
This unit asks students to read colour/pattern/painting symbols beside postmodern practice.

cards: Sherman’s photo roles show identity shaped by media and gaze.

units.title: Ming–Qing Art (1): The Wu School
units.intro: Elective unit. Meet the Ming literati painters of Suzhou, Shen Zhou and Wen Zhengming, and learn to read handscrolls, inscriptions and seals. Matches F.6 Contextual Studies 'Ming–Qing art 1: Shen Zhou, Wen Zhengming'. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Intro to Ming–Qing Art: What Is Literati Painting?
cards: The Ming dynasty (1368–1644) and Qing dynasty (1644–1912) together last almost 550 years — a key period for Chinese painting.
Literati painting (文人畫) is painting by scholars. They did not paint to make a living; they painted to show their feelings and learning.
Literati painting combines four things in one work: poetry, calligraphy, painting and seals (詩書畫印).
Early Ming court painters and the Zhe School (浙派, e.g. Dai Jin 戴進) used bold, showy brushwork; the Wu School (吳門) literati preferred a quiet, refined style.
Class task: in your visual diary, note three 'literati' features you notice, e.g. empty space, inscriptions, pale ink.

quiz.question: Who mainly made literati paintings?
quiz.explain: Literati painting was made by scholars to show their learning and feelings.

quiz.question: Literati painting combines poetry, calligraphy, painting and ____.
In about which year did the Ming dynasty begin?
quiz.explain: The Ming began in 1368 and ended in 1644.

quiz.question: Match each school to its style
quiz.explain: Both are Ming schools, but their styles differ.

lessons.title: Shen Zhou: Founder of the Wu School
cards: Shen Zhou (沈周, 1427–1509) came from Suzhou. He never took an official post; he stayed home to read, write poems and paint.
He is seen as the founder of the Wu School. He learned from the great Yuan painters (the Four Yuan Masters 元四家) and then built his own brush style.
In 1467 he painted Lofty Mount Lu (《廬山高》) for the birthday of his teacher Chen Kuan (陳寬). The tall, layered mountain honours his teacher's character. (National Palace Museum, Taipei)
His early brushwork was fine and careful ('fine Shen' 細沈); after middle age it became broad and bold ('broad Shen' 粗沈).
Class task: copy a small rock in pencil twice — once with 'fine' lines, once with 'broad' lines — and feel the difference.

quiz.question: Did Shen Zhou ever hold an official post?
options: No, he painted and studied at home all his life
quiz.answer: No, he painted and studied at home all his life
quiz.explain: Shen Zhou never served as an official — a typical literati painter.

quiz.question: Who did Shen Zhou paint Lofty Mount Lu for?
quiz.explain: Painted in 1467 for his teacher Chen Kuan's birthday.

quiz.question: Shen Zhou's later bold brushwork is called '____ Shen'.
Which painters did Shen Zhou mainly learn from?
quiz.explain: He carried on the Yuan literati landscape tradition.

lessons.title: Wen Zhengming and the 'Four Masters of the Ming'
cards: Wen Zhengming (文徵明, 1470–1559) was Shen Zhou's student and became famous for both calligraphy and painting.
He failed the civil-service exams many times. In 1523 he went to Beijing as an attendant (待詔) at the Hanlin Academy, but resigned about three years later and returned to Suzhou.
In 1533 he made an album of a friend's garden, the Humble Administrator's Garden (拙政園), with one painting and one poem for each scene. The garden still exists in Suzhou.

The 'Four Masters of the Ming' (明四家) are Shen Zhou, Wen Zhengming, Tang Yin and Qiu Ying (仇英). The first three were scholars; Qiu Ying was a professional painter known for fine detail and blue-green landscapes.
Class task: like Wen Zhengming's 'one scene, one picture, one poem', sketch a small corner near school or home and add one line of text.

quiz.question: How were Wen Zhengming and Shen Zhou related?
quiz.explain: Wen learned from Shen and led the next generation of the Wu School.

quiz.question: Match each painter to a feature
quiz.explain: Each of the Four Masters has a distinct feature.

quiz.question: Wen Zhengming painted an album of the Humble ____'s Garden.
Who is NOT one of the Four Masters of the Ming?
quiz.explain: Qi Baishi is a modern painter, not one of the Four Masters.

lessons.title: How to Read a Literati Painting: Formats, Inscriptions, Seals
cards: Common Chinese painting formats: handscroll (手卷 — horizontal, unrolled right to left), hanging scroll (立軸), album leaf (冊頁) and fan (扇面).
Inscriptions and colophons (題跋) are words written on or beside the painting — the painter's own poem, or later viewers' comments.
Seals come in two kinds: red characters (朱文, 'red-text') and white characters on a red ground (白文, 'white-text'). Collectors stamp seals too, so one painting can carry many.
Landscapes often use the 'three distances' (三遠): high distance (looking up), deep distance (looking in), level distance (looking far across). Empty space (留白) can mean sky, water or mist.
Class task: make a mini handscroll from an A4 sheet — three scenes right to left, one line of inscription, and your own seal design.

quiz.question: How do you view a handscroll?
options: Tear it open left to right
Unroll it slowly from right to left
quiz.answer: Unroll it slowly from right to left
quiz.explain: A handscroll is horizontal and viewed right to left.

quiz.question: Match each seal type
quiz.explain: Red-text: red characters; white-text: white characters.

quiz.question: The 'three distances' are high, deep and ____ distance.
What does empty space in a landscape often stand for?
quiz.explain: Empty space is deliberate, not unfinished.

units.title: Self, Chinese Tradition and Society
units.intro: Elective unit. Through Tang Yin, Chen Chun, Xu Wei, Bada Shanren, Chen Hongshou and Wu Bin, see how artists used painting to express the self and respond to society. Links to DSE work 1 (ink + mixed media, life-size 2D). F.6 theme: How Society and traditional Chinese Heritage influence ordinary life. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Tang Yin: A Talented Scholar's Setback and Self-Image
cards: Tang Yin (唐寅, 1470–1524), also called Tang Bohu (唐伯虎), came from Suzhou. He is the 'Tang Bohu' of popular stories and films.
In 1499 he took the exams in Beijing and was caught up in a cheating scandal. He was barred from office for life — this changed everything.
Afterwards he lived by selling paintings. He even carved a seal reading 'The Most Romantic Talent South of the River' (江南第一風流才子), mocking himself to express who he was.

Autumn Wind and Silk Fan (《秋風紈扇圖》, Shanghai Museum) shows a woman holding a fan in the autumn wind. A fan is useless in autumn, so it is read as being cast aside — and as Tang Yin's own disappointment.
Think: how is the real Tang Yin different from the film 'Tang Bohu'? How can society rewrite an artist's image?

quiz.question: What happened to Tang Yin in 1499?
options: He was caught in an exam-cheating scandal and barred from office
quiz.answer: He was caught in an exam-cheating scandal and barred from office
quiz.explain: The exam scandal ended his official career.

quiz.question: Tang Yin's seal reads 'The Most ____ Talent South of the River'.
How is Autumn Wind and Silk Fan often read?
options: As feeling cast aside and disappointed
quiz.answer: As feeling cast aside and disappointed
quiz.explain: A fan in autumn is unwanted — a metaphor for being neglected.

quiz.question: After losing his chance of office, how did Tang Yin mainly live?
quiz.explain: He made a living from painting and calligraphy.

lessons.title: Chen Chun and Xu Wei: The Freedom of Expressive Ink
cards: Chen Chun (陳淳, 1484–1544), art name Baiyang (白陽), studied with Wen Zhengming. His flowers use quick brushwork and wet ink, moving towards free 'xieyi' (寫意) painting.
Xu Wei (徐渭, 1521–1593), art name Qingteng (青藤), had a hard life: he failed the exams many times and was once imprisoned. He poured his frustration into brush and ink.
Xu Wei's Ink Grapes (《墨葡萄圖》, Palace Museum, Beijing) dots grapes with broad, wet ink. His poem says his talent, like 'bright pearls', was left unwanted among wild vines.
Xu Wei ranked himself 'calligraphy first, poetry second, prose third, painting fourth' — his painting cannot be separated from his writing.
Later critics paired them as 'Qingteng and Baiyang' (青藤白陽). Their bold expressive ink (大寫意) influenced Bada Shanren, the Yangzhou Eccentrics and even Qi Baishi.

quiz.question: Match each painter to his art name
quiz.explain: Together they are called 'Qingteng and Baiyang'.

quiz.question: What does the poem on Ink Grapes express?

lessons.title: Bada Shanren: Rolling Eyes, Strange Rocks and Symbols
cards: Bada Shanren (八大山人, Zhu Da 朱耷, c.1626–1705) was a descendant of the Ming royal family. After the Ming fell he became a Buddhist monk, and later returned to lay life.
His signature 'Bada Shanren' was often written so that it looks like both 'crying over it' (哭之) and 'laughing at it' (笑之) — mixed, complicated feelings.
His birds and fish often roll their eyes upward and hunch their bodies. This is read as defiance towards the new Qing rulers, and loneliness.
His rocks are often top-heavy, as if about to topple, on a nearly empty page with only one or two things — an uneasy feeling.
Class task: choose an animal or object to stand for your mood today. Draw it with very few marks and write one line on what it means.

quiz.question: Who was Bada Shanren?
options: A descendant of the Ming royal family
quiz.answer: A descendant of the Ming royal family
quiz.explain: He was of Ming royal descent and became a monk after the Ming fell.

quiz.question: Bada Shanren's signature looks like 'crying over it' and '____ at it'.

quiz.explain: The rolled eyes are read as defiance and loneliness.

quiz.answer: Empty, with only one or two things
quiz.explain: Large empty space makes the loneliness stronger.

lessons.title: Chen Hongshou and Wu Bin: Figures, Distortion and Strange Stones
cards: Chen Hongshou (陳洪綬, 1598–1652) was a figure painter. His people have big heads, thin bodies and strong drapery lines — deliberately distorted, odd and full of character.
He designed the Water Margin playing cards (《水滸葉子》), turning the heroes of the novel into cards. Figure painting can express identity and character, not just likeness.
He was as famous as Cui Zizhong (崔子忠) in the north: 'Chen of the South, Cui of the North' (南陳北崔).

Wu Bin (吳彬, active c.1583–1626) painted exaggerated, fantastic figures and landscapes. In 1610 he painted Ten Views of a Lingbi Stone (《十面靈璧圖》) for the collector Mi Wanzhong (米萬鍾), showing one rock from ten angles.
Link to DSE work 1: try distortion and exaggeration in a life-size drawing of yourself or a family member, and add one object that stands for their identity (as the stone did for Mi Wanzhong).

options: Deliberately distorted, odd and full of character
quiz.answer: Deliberately distorted, odd and full of character

quiz.answer: One strange rock from ten angles

lessons.title: DSE Work 1: From Research to Life-size Mixed Media
cards: Step 1: Make a mind map on 'Self, Chinese tradition and society' — keywords such as family, community, festivals, traditional objects.
Step 2: Research. Interview family or friends, take photos or sketch; compare at least two artists from this unit (e.g. Xu Wei's ink, Bada's symbols, Chen Hongshou's distortion).
Step 3: Ink experiments. Try dark ink, pale ink, broken ink (破墨) and dry brush, then add collage, paper, fabric and other mixed media.
Step 4: Finish a life-size 2D work, then present it in the 6 sections your teacher sets (e.g. theme, research, experiments, development, final work, reflection).
Reminder: study artists to learn methods, not to copy their style. Record every idea and change in your visual diary.

units.title: Traditional Chinese Symbols: Colour, Pattern and Painting
units.intro: Elective unit. Learn traditional Chinese colours, auspicious patterns, the Four Monks and the Four Wangs, then see how contemporary artists borrow these symbols. Matches F.6 'Sign and symbol in traditional Chinese Heritage' and 'Ming–Qing art 2: literati painting, Four Monks, Four Wangs'. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: What Colours Mean: Five Colours and Status
cards: Ancient China explained the world with the Five Phases (五行): wood, fire, earth, metal, water. Each matches a colour: blue-green, red, yellow, white, black — the 'Five Colours' (五色).
Yellow stands for the centre and earth. In the Qing dynasty, bright yellow (明黃) was reserved for the emperor; ordinary people could not use it freely.
Red means celebration and good luck, so it is used at New Year and weddings; white was traditionally used at funerals.
Colour meanings change with time and place — for example, Western brides wear white. Always read colour together with its context.
Class task: find three things with traditional colours at home or on the street (e.g. New Year couplets, red packets, temples). Photograph or sketch them and note their meaning.

quiz.question: In the Qing dynasty, who was bright yellow reserved for?
quiz.explain: Bright yellow was the emperor's colour.

quiz.question: Match each phase to its colour
quiz.explain: Each of the Five Phases has a colour.

quiz.question: Chinese New Year and weddings often use ____ for celebration.
quiz.explain: Red means celebration and good luck.

quiz.question: What should you consider when reading colour symbols?
options: The context of time and place
quiz.answer: The context of time and place
quiz.explain: The same colour can mean different things in different cultures.

lessons.title: Auspicious Patterns: Sound-alikes and Meanings
cards: Many Chinese patterns use sound-alike words (諧音) for good luck: 'bat' (蝠 fu) sounds like 'blessing' (福 fu); 'fish' (魚 yu) sounds like 'surplus' (餘 yu), as in 'surplus every year'.
'Deer' (鹿 lu) sounds like 'official salary' (祿 lu); 'vase' (瓶 ping) sounds like 'peace' (平 ping).

Plants have meanings too: plum, orchid, bamboo and chrysanthemum are the 'Four Gentlemen' (四君子), standing for noble character; pine, bamboo and plum are the 'Three Friends of Winter' (歲寒三友), standing for endurance in hard times.
These patterns appear on porcelain, clothing, buildings, New Year prints — and today's designs and brands.
Class task: design an 'auspicious pattern' that represents you, using a sound-alike or a symbolic meaning, and write down your design idea.

quiz.question: Match each image to its meaning

quiz.explain: The Four Gentlemen stand for noble character.

quiz.question: Pine, bamboo and plum are the '____ Friends of Winter'.
What does a vase pattern often mean?

lessons.title: The Four Monks of the Early Qing: Individuality and Innovation
cards: After the Ming fell, four painters who had been Buddhist monks became known as the 'Four Monks' (清初四僧): Hongren, Kuncan, Bada Shanren and Shitao.
Hongren (弘仁, 1610–1664) often painted Mount Huang with clean lines and simple structure; Kuncan (髡殘, born 1612) painted dense, heavy landscapes.
Shitao (石濤, 1642–1707) was also born into the Ming royal clan. He said 'search out all the strange peaks to make sketches' (搜盡奇峰打草稿) — observe nature yourself.
Shitao also said 'brush and ink should follow the times' (筆墨當隨時代): methods should change with the age, not just copy the ancients. This still inspires artists today.
The Four Monks valued personal feeling and innovation — a contrast with the Four Wangs in the next lesson, who valued learning from the old masters.

quiz.explain: Wang Hui is one of the Four Wangs.

quiz.question: Shitao said 'brush and ink should follow the ____'.
quiz.explain: Methods should change with the age.

quiz.question: What does 'search out all the strange peaks to make sketches' mean?
options: Observe many real landscapes yourself before creating
quiz.answer: Observe many real landscapes yourself before creating

quiz.explain: Each monk had a strong personal style.

lessons.title: The Four Wangs of the Early Qing: Learning from the Past
cards: The 'Four Wangs' (四王) — Wang Shimin (王時敏), Wang Jian (王鑑), Wang Hui (王翬) and Wang Yuanqi (王原祁) — were seen as the 'orthodox' school of early Qing painting.
They followed the late-Ming critic Dong Qichang (董其昌, 1555–1636), who divided landscape painting into 'Southern' and 'Northern' schools and praised the literati Southern School.
The Four Wangs valued 'imitating the ancients' (仿古): studying old masters' brushwork closely and recombining it. Many works are inscribed 'after the brush manner of …'.
Wang Hui led the painting of the Kangxi Emperor's Southern Inspection Tour scrolls (《康熙南巡圖》). With court support, their style was hugely influential.
Compare: the Four Monks valued individuality; the Four Wangs valued learning from the past. Both can inspire you — do you want to learn tradition, or express yourself, or both?

quiz.question: Who belongs to the Four Wangs?
quiz.explain: Wang Shimin was the senior of the Four Wangs.

quiz.question: Dong Qichang divided landscape painting into Southern and ____ schools.
quiz.explain: The Southern and Northern schools theory.

quiz.question: What did the Four Wangs value most?
options: Imitating and learning from old masters
quiz.answer: Imitating and learning from old masters
quiz.explain: Learning from the ancients was central.

quiz.question: Match each group to its attitude

lessons.title: Postmodernism: How Contemporary Artists Borrow Traditional Symbols
cards: Postmodern art often uses appropriation: putting old images and symbols into a new context so we rethink what they mean.

Qiu Zhijie (邱志杰), Writing the 'Orchid Pavilion Preface' One Thousand Times (1990–1995): he wrote the famous calligraphy text over and over on one sheet until it turned black — tradition becomes a work about time and repetition.
Xu Bing (徐冰), Book from the Sky (《天書》, 1987–1991): thousands of carved 'characters' that look Chinese but cannot be read, making us question language and culture.

Ding Yi (丁乙) has painted his 'Appearance of Crosses' (十示) series since 1988, repeating '+' and '×'; Lam Tung-pang (林東鵬) mixes traditional landscape composition with Hong Kong memories on plywood; Wilson Shieh (石家豪) paints contemporary figures in gongbi.
Note: contemporary works are under copyright, so the platform shows no images. Please view them on the museums' official websites.

quiz.question: What does 'appropriation' mean?
options: Putting old images into a new context to create new meaning
quiz.answer: Putting old images into a new context to create new meaning
quiz.explain: Appropriation is a common postmodern strategy.

units.title: Role-taking: Re-presenting Someone in a Chinese Context
units.intro: Elective unit. From Cindy Sherman's role-play to the figures and self-images of the Yangzhou Eccentrics, Xu Beihong and Qi Baishi, learn to 're-present someone in a Chinese context'. Links to DSE work 2 (dry/wet media drawing and painting). Matches F.6 Role taking (Part 3) and 'Ming–Qing art: Yangzhou Eccentrics, Xu Beihong, Qi Baishi'. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Cindy Sherman and Wang Qingsong: Role-play and Restaging
cards: American artist Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977–1980) is a series of about 70 black-and-white photographs. Sherman is her own model, dressed as different female characters from films.
The characters look familiar, but they come from no real film. Sherman makes us ask: how do films and media shape images of women?

Wang Qingsong (王慶松), Night Revels of Lao Li (《老栗夜宴圖》, 2000), restages the classic Night Revels of Han Xizai (《韓熙載夜宴圖》, attributed to Gu Hongzhong 顧閎中) as a photograph, with art critic Li Xianting (栗憲庭) in the main role, to comment on today's society.
Both use role-play and restaging: borrow a familiar image, put it in a new context, and raise questions about identity and society.
Note: both are contemporary artists whose works are under copyright, so the platform shows no images. View them on official sites such as MoMA and Tate.

quiz.explain: Role-play raises questions of identity and society.

lessons.title: The Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou: What Made Them 'Eccentric'?
cards: In the mid-Qing, Yangzhou grew rich from the salt trade and drew many painters to sell their work. A group with new, unusual styles became known as the 'Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou' (揚州八怪). (The scheme of work writes 楊州; the correct form is 揚州.)

Lists of the 'Eight' vary. Common names: Jin Nong (金農), Zheng Xie (鄭燮, Zheng Banqiao), Huang Shen (黃慎), Li Shan (李鱓), Li Fangying (李方膺), Wang Shishen (汪士慎), Gao Xiang (高翔) and Luo Pin (羅聘); some lists add Hua Yan (華嵒) and others.

Zheng Xie loved painting bamboo, invented his own 'six-and-a-half' script (六分半書), and wrote 'it is hard to be muddle-headed' (難得糊塗). As a county magistrate, his bamboo poem says even small officials care about every branch and leaf — he cared for ordinary people.
Jin Nong painted self-portraits; his student Luo Pin painted his teacher's portrait and the Ghost Amusements scroll (《鬼趣圖》), using ghosts to mock society.
Think: why were they called 'eccentric'? Their methods, their personalities, or refusing to follow the mainstream?

quiz.question: Why did Qing Yangzhou attract many painters?
options: Rich salt merchants made a big art market
quiz.answer: Rich salt merchants made a big art market
quiz.explain: The salt economy made the art market thrive.

quiz.question: Who wrote 'it is hard to be muddle-headed' (難得糊塗)?
quiz.explain: A famous saying of Zheng Banqiao.

quiz.explain: Each Eccentric had his own character.

lessons.title: Xu Beihong: Telling His Times Through Figures
cards: Xu Beihong (徐悲鴻, 1895–1953) studied Western drawing and oil painting in France and argued for using realism to reform Chinese painting.
In 1940, at Visva-Bharati University in India (founded by Rabindranath Tagore), he painted the large ink work The Foolish Old Man Who Removed the Mountains (《愚公移山》) and also a portrait of Tagore.
The work uses an ancient fable and shows strong labourers. During the war against Japan it spread the message: keep going and you will succeed.
He combined Western anatomy and drawing with Chinese brush lines — a good example of re-presenting someone in a Chinese context.
Class task: choose a fable or historical story, use someone near you as the model, and redraw one character.

options: Keep going and you will succeed
quiz.answer: Keep going and you will succeed
quiz.explain: An old fable used to lift people's spirits.

quiz.answer: Western drawing combined with Chinese brushwork
quiz.explain: Realist figures blending Chinese and Western methods.

lessons.title: Qi Baishi: From Carpenter to Master, 'Between Likeness and Unlikeness'
cards: Qi Baishi (齊白石, 1864–1957) grew up in rural Hunan and worked as a carpenter when young. He taught himself poetry, calligraphy, painting and seal carving.

From around 1917, encouraged by his friend Chen Shizeng (陳師曾), he 'changed his style in old age' (衰年變法): in his fifties he boldly changed, learning from the bold ink of Xu Wei, Bada Shanren and Wu Changshuo.
He often paired finely detailed insects with loose, bold leaves and flowers ('fine and free combined', 工寫結合); 'red flowers, ink leaves' (紅花墨葉) is another trademark.
He said: 'The wonder of painting lies between likeness and unlikeness. Too alike flatters vulgar taste; too unlike deceives the world.' Don't only chase likeness — but don't lose it completely.
Link: Qi painted everyday small things — shrimps, cabbages, chicks. Ordinary life can become important art.

lessons.title: DSE Work 2: Re-presenting Someone with Dry and Wet Media
cards: Title: Reappear someone in Chinese context. First choose a person: a family member, friend, historical figure, or a role you play yourself.
Wet media: ink, watercolour, acrylic — good for washes, large areas and mood. Dry media: charcoal, pencil, pastel, coloured pencil — good for line, texture and detail.
Try mixing them: e.g. lay a pale ink wash first, then strengthen outlines with charcoal. Like Sherman, you can stage and photograph a role-play for reference.
Add a Chinese context: clothing, objects, auspicious symbols, composition (e.g. handscroll or hanging-scroll format), or restage an old painting.
Afterwards, make a mind map and a critique of your own work: which part works best? What could improve?

units.title: British YBAs and Contemporary Art: Connecting with Chinese Art
units.intro: Elective unit. Meet the 1990s Young British Artists (YBAs), then compare them with Chinese and Hong Kong contemporary artists. Matches F.6 Contextual Studies 'British YBA Art' and 'how YBA, American art relate to Chinese Art'. All works here are contemporary, so there are no images — only text descriptions and official museum links. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: What Are the YBAs?
cards: YBA means Young British Artists — a group who rose in London in the late 1980s and 1990s.

In 1988, while still a student at Goldsmiths College in London, Damien Hirst organised the exhibition 'Freeze' with fellow students in an empty building in London's Docklands. It is seen as the YBAs' starting point.
Collector Charles Saatchi bought many of their works. In 1997 the Royal Academy of Arts in London showed his collection in 'Sensation', which caused great controversy.
YBA features: unexpected materials (animals, beds, everyday objects), shock effects, organising their own shows, and skill with the media.
Think: is shock the aim of art in itself, or a way to make people think?

quiz.question: What does YBA stand for?

quiz.explain: 'Freeze' is seen as the YBAs' start.

quiz.explain: Saatchi's collection was later shown in 'Sensation'.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a common YBA feature?
quiz.explain: YBAs stressed new materials and shock.

lessons.title: Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin: Death and Private Life
cards: Damien Hirst's 1991 work The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living suspends a real tiger shark in formaldehyde in a glass tank, asking how we face death.
Hirst's spot paintings arrange coloured dots in neat grids; many were made by assistants, raising the question 'who is the author?'. He won the Turner Prize in 1995.
Tracey Emin's My Bed (1998) shows her own messy bed and the things around it — the real state of a low period in her life. It was shortlisted for the Turner Prize in 1999.
Emin also uses neon text and embroidery to write very personal sentences, making diary-like feelings public.
Note: these works are under copyright. See images and texts on Tate's official website.

lessons.title: Rachel Whiteread and Gillian Wearing: Space and Identity
cards: Rachel Whiteread casts space itself: the inside of a wardrobe, the space under a bath, the gaps of a staircase, turned into solid sculpture — the invisible becomes visible.
Her House (1993) cast the inside of a condemned house in East London in concrete; it was demolished in 1994. That year, 1993, Whiteread became the first woman to win the Turner Prize.

In 1992–93 Gillian Wearing asked strangers on the street to write what they wanted to say on a sheet of white paper and photographed them (Signs that say what you want them to say…), letting ordinary people speak their real minds. She won the Turner Prize in 1997.
Later, Wearing used masks to 'play' her family members and herself at different ages — compare this with Cindy Sherman's role-play.
Think: Whiteread shows us emptiness; Wearing shows us honest words. What do you want viewers to see in your work?

lessons.title: Reading YBAs, American Art and Chinese Art Together
cards: Hirst ↔ Huang Yong Ping (黃永砅): both use real animals or living things. Huang's Theater of the World (1993) puts insects and reptiles together in one cage to survive side by side — a metaphor for conflict in the world.

Emin ↔ Song Dong (宋冬): Emin shows her own bed; Song Dong's Waste Not (2005) shows over ten thousand everyday things his mother kept for decades. Both use private belongings to speak about identity and memory.
Wearing ↔ Pak Sheung Chuen (白雙全): both care about ordinary people and daily life, making work from simple actions or records.

American Pop ↔ Chinese Political Pop: Andy Warhol repeated images of products and celebrities; Wang Guangyi (王廣義) set Cultural Revolution poster imagery beside Western brands, responding to consumer society.
Method: describe the works first, then fill three columns — similar, different, what you can borrow — instead of just saying which is 'better'.
